Once again, young, promising lives have been brutally cut short on a public road not by inevitable natural catastrophe, but by the reckless, high-speed aggression that has come to define political motorcades in Nigeria. While official statements offer habitual condolences and promises of police investigations, the grieving families are left to confront a painful reality: our public highways have been effectively converted into private hazard zones for state officials.
Over the years, executive convoy driving in Nigeria has degenerated into an intolerable display of elitist arrogance and institutional lawlessness. Sirens blare furiously, heavily armed security escorts brandish weapons at frightened motorists, and heavy government vehicles force oncoming traffic off narrow, single-lane roads in a desperate hurry to clear paths for public officers. This dangerous culture reflects a deep-seated administrative posture that treats the convenience of political office holders as superior to the very lives of the citizens they were elected to serve.
The moral absurdity of this highway menace is laid bare when contrasted with the treatment meted out to ordinary Nigerians in dire emergencies. Across urban gridlocks and inter-state corridors, ambulances carrying patients in critical condition are routinely left trapped in traffic, their blaring sirens ignored by indifferent motorists and traffic wardens alike. Yet, the moment a government official approaches, armed security details aggressively split traffic, force vehicles into ditches, and unleash terrifying physical intimidation to secure an unobstructed passage. It is a damning indictment of our social values that state apparatuses mobilize immense authority to facilitate the movement of politicians, while ordinary citizens fighting for survival in emergency vehicles are left to perish in traffic congestion.
The human cost of this reckless culture is staggering and tragically recurring. Beyond the civilian casualties who are maimed or killed when government vehicles execute unlawful overtaking manoeuvres, the motorcades themselves are frequently caught in the carnage. Over the decades, scores of security aides, official drivers, journalists, and support staff attached to state governors, ministers, and political figures have suffered severe injuries or lost their lives in fatal convoy roll-overs triggered by excessive speed. When a government motorcade cannot even guarantee the safety of its own occupants, its operation ceases to be a functional security protocol and becomes a clear public danger.
This culture of impunity persists because executive drivers and their political principals operate under the delusion of immunity from traffic laws. While Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution protects specific executive office holders from criminal prosecution while in office, that legal shield was never intended to cover government drivers, security escorts, or official motorcades operating with fatal disregard for road safety codes. A motor vehicle traveling at extreme speeds on a public highway is a lethal weapon, and those who operate them recklessly must be held accountable to the full extent of the law.
We at LEADERSHIP firmly asserts that this systemic horror on our highways must stop immediately. The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) must abandon its passive posture toward official motorcades and actively enforce national speed limits and lane discipline on all government convoys without exception. The FRSC and the Nigeria Police Force must begin the swift prosecution of all errant official drivers involved in traffic violations or fatal road crashes, establishing clear legal precedents that state employment provides zero cover for criminal negligence.
Furthermore, state governments must urgently formulate, publish, and enforce strict convoy safety protocols. Governors and administrative heads must mandate that their drivers observe statutory speed limits, respect civil traffic controls, and end the aggressive intimidation of road users. Beyond criminal prosecution of drivers, state governments must accept vicarious liability, while political office holders whose motorcades cause civilian casualties must be held personally and civilly liable for damages. The lives of Nigerian citizens are not disposable collateral for official mobility, and state power must no longer be driven down our highways with deadly arrogance.
